newsitem.title: UK: Britain appoints two new Bank of England deputies.
newsitem.headline: Britain appoints two new Bank of England deputies.

text.p: Britain's Labour government reinforced its pro-business credentials and pleased financial markets on Thursday with its choice of two new deputy governors for the Bank of England.
The deputies will take seats on the interest rate-setting Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) and will assist central bank Governor Eddie George.
The first, David Clementi, is a top investment banker and architect of Conservative privatisations whose appointment to the central bank was widely expected following weekend press leaks.
But the second, the central bank's chief economist and arch-inflation hawk Mervyn King, came as an unexpected and welcome surprise in financial circles.
Analysts say the new appointments mean that once all nine members of the MPC finally join later this year, there will be a distinct anti-inflation bias.
The next meeting is scheduled for August 6 and 7 and there is speculation that official interest rates will rise from 6.75 percent to 7.0 percent -- the fourth quarter-point rise in as many months.
Clementi, 48, will join in time for the September 10/11 meeting, at the same time as DeAnne Julius of British Airways .

But it was King, already a member of the MPC, who will grab the headlines. "He's built himself a good reputation for being tough on inflation and the markets trust him," one ex-Bank of England official said.

King's profile has increased markedly since the Bank began publishing quarterly assessments of the British inflation environment in February 1993 and holding on-the-record briefings on its view of the economy.
Some City insiders said he could have left the Bank if passed over for a deputy governorship.
There was less comment on the appointment of Clementi for the simple reason that little is known of his attitude to the economy.
At the moment, the financial markets are taking his leading role in the former Conservative administration's 1980s privatisation programme as a sign that he is likely to be another inflation hawk.
Clementi succeeds Howard Davies who is leaving to head revamped City watchdog, the Securities and Investment Board (SIB).
He spent 22 years at merchant bank Kleinwort Benson, including three years as chief executive, which culminated in his appointment as vice chairman this year.

As leader of the day-to-day team responsible for advising Margaret Thatcher's Conservative government on privatisation, Clementi spearheaded the sales of British Telecom, British Gas and the privatisation of the electricity industry.
Born in Bury, Northern England, he trained as a chartered accountant with Arthur Andersen and has an MBA from Harvard Business School.
Former Bank of England officials say his job is the less glamorous of the two deputy governor positions.
King will be responsible "for analysis and advice in relation to the bank's responsibilities for delivering the government's inflation target," Blair's office said.
He has been with the central bank for seven years and was previously professor of economics at the London School of Economics.

But in taking over from Davies as head of internal management at the central bank -- effectively a chief executive's role -- Clementi will have more than enough to do overseeing the current reorganisation of the Bank.
While giving control of interest rates with one hand, Brown took with the other, transferring much of the Bank's regulatory role to the SIB, while giving the Treasury control of debt management.

Clementi's move from the private to the public sector will mean a substantial pay cut, but his deputy governor's salary of 184,000 pounds ($300,000) per year is still more than 10 times the national average wage. ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
